cases.original_authored_answer:
Counter stores hashable elements as keys and permits zero or negative counts. Looking up a missing element returns zero, while setting an existing count to zero leaves the entry present. update adds counts instead of replacing them, and subtract can retain zero or negative results.

Multiset subtraction has a different output policy: like the other multiset operations, it excludes nonpositive results. elements requires integer counts and ignores those below one. Equality treats absent elements as zero, so Counter(a=1) equals Counter(a=1, b=0). Equal-count entries in most_common keep their first-encountered order.

cases.question: How should cancellation and failures be handled inside an asyncio TaskGroup?
cases.question_origin: AI data-author practical question, not a recorded production user
cases.input_adapter: Question: {question}\n\nAnswer: {unmodified_authored_answer}; question is visible but never source evidence
cases.original_authored_answer:
Cancellation raises CancelledError in a task at its next opportunity. That exception directly subclasses BaseException; coroutine cleanup should generally propagate it after cleanup, because TaskGroup and timeout use cancellation internally. A TaskGroup waits for all its tasks on exit, and in Python 3.13 an inactive group closes a coroutine passed to create_task.

The first child failure other than CancelledError cancels the remaining children and prevents new additions. Once all children finish, non-cancellation failures are grouped and raised. KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit are special: the group still cancels and waits for the other tasks but re-raises the original base exception. A simultaneous external cancellation is preserved by cancelling the parent task when the group must also raise an ExceptionGroup.

cases.input_adapter: Question: {question}\n\nAnswer: {unmodified_authored_answer}; question is visible but never source evidence
cases.original_authored_answer:
--proxy uses HTTP when no scheme is supplied and assumes port 1080 if none is specified. It overrides proxy environment variables; an empty proxy string can disable a proxy inherited from the environment. --noproxy takes comma-separated host rules, with a single * matching every host, and can override no_proxy and NO_PROXY.

A domain rule local.com also matches its subdomains but not notlocal.com. A preproxy connects through SOCKS first and then to the specified HTTP or HTTPS proxy. --socks5 resolves the target hostname locally. Usernames and passwords embedded in a proxy URL are URL-decoded, and hiding --proxy-user from process listings is not sufficient to prevent a brief exposure.

cases.question: How should curl resume or retrieve partial files, and what happens to the local output on an error?
cases.question_origin: AI data-author practical question, not a recorded production user
cases.input_adapter: Question: {question}\n\nAnswer: {unmodified_authored_answer}; question is visible but never source evidence
cases.original_authored_answer:
--continue-at resumes from a byte offset measured from the beginning of the source; -C - derives the resume point from the input or output file. --range can request the first 500 bytes as 0-499 or the last 500 as -500. A server without HTTP range support may return the whole document.

Multiple HTTP ranges produce a multipart response that curl returns unchanged for the caller to parse. FTP and SFTP only support the simple start-stop form, with either end optionally omitted. --output associates its first filename with the first URL regardless of their command-line order. --remove-on-error deletes a failed transfer output only when it is a regular file, so it does not clean up arbitrary output targets.

cases.question: How can curl multipart form input distinguish literal text, files and streams that cannot be buffered?
cases.question_origin: AI data-author practical question, not a recorded production user
cases.input_adapter: Question: {question}\n\nAnswer: {unmodified_authored_answer}; question is visible but never source evidence
cases.original_authored_answer:
--form sends HTTP multipart/form-data. Prefixing a value with @ attaches a file, while < reads file contents into a text field. For either form, a filename of - reads stdin and buffers it in memory to determine size and permit a possible resend.

A named nonregular file is instead read during transmission without that buffering; its unknown size makes HTTP send chunks and IMAP reject it. --form-string treats leading @, < and ;type= literally, avoiding accidental file semantics. filename= can change the upload part name, while --form-escape changes field and filename escaping from percent encoding to backslash escaping. A base64 transfer encoder limits encoded lines to 76 characters.
